extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century periodical essays; general literate public interested in literature, moral reflection, and the Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Composing short moral, imaginative, and observational essays for a periodical—using poetic and rhetorical examples, anecdotes, and moral reflections to please and instruct a polite reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness (the Sublime) as a source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness is one of the sources of the pleasures of the imagination; vast objects like the sea or ocean produce a high kind of pleasure derived from their magnitude and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large, awe-inspiring objects or scenes (e.g., the ocean in a tempest) to move the imagination and to prompt grand ideas (such as the existence of an Almighty Being). The author uses the sea as an example of how Greatness elevates the mind and produces sublime pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather circumstances that most affect the imagination; avoid 'little fancies'
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective sublime description arises when the writer 'gathers together those Circumstances which are the most apt to terrify the Imagination' rather than amusing the reader with little fancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing a grand or terrifying scene (e.g., a ship in a storm), assemble vivid, relevant particulars that contribute directly to terror or awe; do not dilute the effect with trivial, distracting details. The passage cites Longinus's praise of Homer for this economy and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer coherent, elevated moral/philosophical framing in sublime depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A description that unifies natural spectacle with a single, elevated moral or theological conception (as in the Psalmist) is nobler and more satisfactory than fragmented or contradictory mythic attributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame sublime events within a coherent worldview (the example contrasts the Psalmist's single divine agent controlling the storm with pagan depictions where different deities contradict one another). Such unity enhances the effect and the moral resonance of the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrich essays with cross-media examples (painting, poetry, music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writers often borrow examples and modes from other arts—painters' sea-pieces, odes, and music can illustrate and augment an essay on imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate or allude to painting, poetry, and even musical settings (the author suggests appending a divine ode set to music) to provide varied, concrete illustrations that deepen the essay's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use true, authoritative stories to feed the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories 'for the Truth of which there is good Authority' are especially pleasing because the mind loves justice and moral order; authentic-seeming narratives serve as food for the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select anecdotes or tales grounded in credible authority; readers derive satisfaction from morally charged stories where wrongdoing is punished and justice is served. The author introduces a historical narrative (Rhynsault and Danvelt) to exemplify this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide moral resolution—depict criminals being overtaken
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind naturally loves justice; when reading a story wherein a criminal is overtaken, the reader experiences a pleasurable sense of revenge and moral satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure narratives to include moral closure or retribution when appropriate, since such outcomes gratify readers' sense of justice and enhance the emotional payoff of a tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage readers with contributions (poems/epigrams) and acknowledge authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Include and credit reader-submitted verses or epigrams in the periodical to build literary conversation and acknowledge contributors (example: printing Mr. Tate's epigram and returning thanks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing readers' literary contributions and citing their names (or acknowledging anonymous composers) fosters engagement and provides variety of content; it also situates the periodical within a network of contemporary writers and composers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical publishing/marketing measures for periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: To alleviate the expense to readers, propose retrenchment of small household items or offer the paper in collected volumes (sold 'in the lump') and in portable, giftable formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested tactics include urging readers to sacrifice minor daily luxuries to afford the paper, and offering collected volumes in small portable formats marketed as suitable gifts for christenings, marriages, visiting-days, etc. The bookseller's practice of issuing bound volumes is given as an example of widening readership and easing per-issue cost.
